The factor theorem gives f(x)=x²+k(x−2)(x−3)(x−4), where k≠0 because the degree is 3. The secant through (a,a²) and (b,b²) is L(x)=(a+b)x−ab, so x²−L(x)=(x−a)(x−b). If c is the remaining member of {2,3,4}, then f(x)−L(x)=(x−a)(x−b)[1+k(x−c)], and the extra intersection has x-coordinate c−1/k. The three extra coordinates sum to 9−3/k=24, yielding k=−1/5 and f(0)=−24k=24/5. Alternatively, each secant subtraction preserves the cubic and quadratic coefficients, so cubic root sums give the same equations. Both proposed routes are valid.

A valid arbitrary-angle addition-identity proof is sin x+sin y−sin(x+y)=sin x(1−cos y)+sin y(1−cos x). For x,y∈[0,π], both sine factors and both factors 1−cos are nonnegative, so the inequality holds throughout the entire closed interval, including its endpoints. The supplied support nodes cover these sign and range comparisons. Whether the addition-identity step already has a suitable catalog scope cannot be determined from the supplied definitions.

Apart from measure-zero endpoints, 1 is the longest side. The triangle condition reduces to x+y>1. By the cosine law, its opposite angle is obtuse exactly when x²+y²<1. The favorable region is therefore the part of the first-quadrant unit disk above x+y=1. Its area is π/4−1/2≈0.285398, closest to 0.29. Because the full sampling square has area 1, this is the unconditional probability; one must not divide by the probability of forming a triangle. The proposed support nodes cover the side conditions, cosine-sign reasoning, and areas, but not the continuous area-ratio probability model.

audits.mathematicalReason: The points in A are 2 and −1±i√3, obtainable either from polar cube roots or from z³−8=(z−2)[(z+1)²+3] and complex factorization. The second polynomial factors as (z−8)(z²−8), so B={8,2√2,−2√2}, all on the real axis. The distance from 8 to either nonreal point of A is √(9²+3)=2√21, whereas its distance to 2 is 6. For either other point of B, the triangle inequality bounds every distance to A by 2+2√2<6. Thus 2√21 is the greatest distance. Both root-finding routes and the common geometric-distance scopes are defensible.

Carlos leaves 1−0.70=0.30 of the whole pie. Maria takes one third of that remainder, leaving two thirds of it: (2/3)·0.30=0.20=20%. The base quantity for Maria's fraction is the remainder, not the whole pie, matching the fraction-of-a-quantity scope.

Classifying by the omitted color gives 8!/(1!3!4!)+8!/(2!2!4!)+8!/(2!3!3!)=280+420+560=1260. These cases are disjoint, and copies of a color are indistinguishable. Alternatively, append the single unused color to the ordered tower. This bijects eligible towers with all nine-position color sequences having multiplicities 2,3,4; deleting the last position is the inverse. Their number is 9!/(2!3!4!)=1260. Both proposed routes are valid without being jointly required.

The exponent of 5 in 15! is 3, and its exponent of 2 is at least 3, so 1000 divides 15!. The same is true of 20!, whose exponent of 5 is 4. Consequently 1000 divides their positive difference, and its hundreds digit is 0. This is a direct factorial-divisibility application of prime valuations.

Let c, a, and d be the corner-hitting probabilities from the center, an axial interior neighbor, and a diagonal interior neighbor. Square symmetry makes these the three interior state types. With boundary values 1 at corners and 0 elsewhere, first-step averaging gives 8c=4a+4d, 8a=c+2a+2d, and 8d=1+c+2a. Solving yields c=4/35, a=1/14, and d=11/70, so m+n=39. Absorption is justified: from every interior position there is probability at least 1/64 of reaching the boundary within two steps, so indefinite survival has probability zero. State recursion, total probability, and a three-variable linear system match the proposed scopes.
